qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The European Commission has announced a Global Gateway package of EUR 200 million for Greenland and the intention to double support to EUR 530 million in the upcoming Multiannual Financial Framework. I welcome any effort by the Union to secure critical resources in the face of global competition and the eagerness to reduce dependence on China! However, while the Commission wants to massively finance the creation of infrastructure from scratch under extreme polar conditions, Member States such as Romania already possess strategic graphite deposits and transport networks, as well as the energy and workforce needed for immediate integration into the European industrial chain. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Why is the Commission granting financial priority to external mining projects in the Arctic instead of making use of graphite deposits in Member States such as Romania, where these deposits can be readily exploited and where the basic infrastructure is already in place?
Are there any contractual clauses obliging mining companies benefiting from EU support in Greenland to prioritise the delivery of the extracted raw materials to industry in the Member States?
How are the Union’s resource exploitation rights guaranteed in the long term in the event that Greenland declares its full independence from Denmark?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.10.2026) In line with the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA)1 and the RESourceEU Action Plan2, the Commission pursues a complementary approach aimed at strengthening the EU’s domestic capacities while diversifying external sources of supply through partnerships with reliable partners. Developing production and processing capacities within the EU is a key priority. Under the CRMA, strategic projects have been designated across the EU, including in Romania3. In parallel, the Commission is mobilising EU instruments to strengthen European raw materials value chains, including for battery raw materials such as graphite. At the same time, projected EU demand for a number of strategic raw materials exceeds existing and planned domestic production capacities. Diversifying external sources of supply therefore complements, rather than substitutes, efforts to develop the EU’s domestic resource base. When assessing strategic raw materials projects, the Commission considers their contribution to strengthening secure and resilient EU value chains, including through relevant offtake arrangements. In this context, the Amitsoq graphite project in Greenland has been recognised as a strategic project under the CRMA, in particular for its expected capacity to secure supply for EU offtakes. The EU’s engagement on raw materials in Greenland takes place in close cooperation with the Greenlandic authorities, which are competent for mineral resources governance, and within the existing framework of the 2023 EU and Greenland strategic partnership on sustainable raw materials value chains4.
